spec.title: Dry-run: multi-channel notification delivery
spec.intro: About 6 minutes. The system is a router with a retry policy bolted on — most of the design is deciding what happens when a channel says no.

steps.title: One event, many channels, one dedup key
steps.explain: A single business event — order shipped — can fan out to push, email, and SMS. The event carries its own dedup key so retries anywhere downstream don't create a second notification for the same fact.
steps.saysOutLoud: The event is the source of truth; channels are just delivery targets for it.

steps.title: Render once per channel, not once total
steps.explain: A push notification is 40 characters; an email is a full HTML template. Rendering is channel-specific, so it happens after the fan-out decision, using a template keyed by event type and channel.

steps.title: Send through the provider, expect it to fail
steps.explain: Providers rate-limit, time out, and occasionally reject a valid token. The send wraps every attempt in a per-channel idempotency key so a retry after a timeout can't double-send if the first attempt actually went through.
steps.saysOutLoud: I always assume the response can be lost even when the send succeeded, so the retry has to be safe.

steps.title: Retry with backoff, then dead-letter
steps.explain: Transient failures — provider 500s, timeouts — get retried with exponential backoff and jitter. A permanent failure — invalid token, unsubscribed user — should not retry at all; retrying those just burns quota for no chance of success.

steps.title: The queue between event and send is the resilience
steps.explain: The producer publishes the event once and returns immediately; a queue (SQS, Kafka) holds it durably while workers do the actual channel fan-out. If a worker crashes mid-send, the message is redelivered and the per-channel idempotency key from the previous step absorbs the duplicate — decoupling the fast path from the slow, failure-prone one.

steps.title: Respect quiet hours and frequency caps before sending
steps.explain: Not every eligible notification should go out immediately — a user's local quiet hours and a per-user rate cap both apply before the send, not after. This is a product decision as much as a technical one, and worth naming as such in an interview.

steps.title: Unsubscribe is a hard stop, checked last
steps.explain: Checking preferences again immediately before the provider call — not just once at fan-out time — closes the window where a user unsubscribes between the event firing and the send actually happening, which matters most for slow channels like email digests.

spec.closing: If they ask about ordering: notifications for the same user can arrive out of channel-order (push before email) because each channel has its own latency and retry path — say plainly that cross-channel ordering isn't guaranteed, only per-channel delivery is idempotent.
